subtitle: Step through 10 turning points of the Islamic Golden Age—from Caliph al-Mansur's Round City, paper mills, and the House of Wisdom to algebra, astrolabes, hospitals, and global legacy.

milestones.title: Caliph al-Mansur Builds the Round City of Baghdad
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did Caliph al-Mansur build Baghdad right where the Tigris and Euphrates rivers ran close together?
milestones.imageCaption: Map of the Round City of Baghdad on the River Tigris and its overland Silk Road and sea trade routes.
milestones.provenance: The History Revision Hub Cartography Studio (Natural Earth 50m)
milestones.catalyst: Choosing the fertile canal crossroads between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur hired 100,000 workers to raise Madinat al-Salam ("City of Peace")—a 2km geometric circle with double mudbrick walls, four compass gates, and the Green Dome palace!
milestones.turningPoint: Children watched round woven quffa coracle boats spin across the sparkling Tigris loaded with dates, melons, and bricks.
milestones.impact: While Anglo-Saxon English towns held only a few thousand people in timber huts, Baghdad boomed toward nearly one million citizens.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 794): Harun al-Rashid’s Golden Court & Baghdad’s First Paper Mills.

ks2.story: Choosing the fertile canal crossroads between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, Abbasid Caliph al-Mansur hired 100,000 workers to raise Madinat al-Salam ("City of Peace")—a 2km geometric circle with double mudbrick walls, four compass gates, and the Green Dome palace!
ks2.significance: While Anglo-Saxon English towns held only a few thousand people in timber huts, Baghdad boomed toward nearly one million citizens.
ks2.childrenLife: Children watched round woven quffa coracle boats spin across the sparkling Tigris loaded with dates, melons, and bricks.
ks2.quote: “Before laying a single brick, surveyors traced Baghdad’s circular walls in cotton seeds lit at night so the Caliph could inspect the circle!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did Caliph al-Mansur build Baghdad right where the Tigris and Euphrates rivers ran close together?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Irrigated canals grew abundant food and boats could sail both inland from Syria and out to the Persian Gulf toward India and China!

milestones.title: Harun al-Rashid’s Golden Court & Baghdad’s First Paper Mills
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did making paper from linen and cotton rags help science spread much faster than animal parchment?
milestones.imageCaption: Abbasid gold dinar coin minted in Baghdad carrying Arabic calligraphy inscriptions.
milestones.provenance: Museum Numismatic Collection / Public Domain (Wikimedia Commons)
milestones.catalyst: Under Caliph Harun al-Rashid, paper-makers brought Central Asian papermaking skills to Baghdad—pounding cotton and linen rags into smooth, affordable sheets that replaced costly sheep-skin parchment!
milestones.turningPoint: Young students practised neat Arabic handwriting with cut reed pens (qalam) on smooth rag paper.
milestones.impact: Cheap paper sparked a reading revolution: Baghdad’s Paper-Sellers’ Market soon boasted over 100 bustling bookshops and public libraries.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 813–833): The House of Wisdom & Multi-Faith Translation Movement.

ks2.story: Under Caliph Harun al-Rashid, paper-makers brought Central Asian papermaking skills to Baghdad—pounding cotton and linen rags into smooth, affordable sheets that replaced costly sheep-skin parchment!
ks2.significance: Cheap paper sparked a reading revolution: Baghdad’s Paper-Sellers’ Market soon boasted over 100 bustling bookshops and public libraries.
ks2.childrenLife: Young students practised neat Arabic handwriting with cut reed pens (qalam) on smooth rag paper.
ks2.quote: “In early medieval Europe one parchment Bible needed hundreds of calfskins; in Baghdad paper mills turned old rags into thousands of books!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did making paper from linen and cotton rags help science spread much faster than animal parchment?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Paper was far cheaper, lighter, and quicker to make than animal skins, so hundreds of copies of books could be shared!

milestones.title: The House of Wisdom & Multi-Faith Translation Movement
milestones.enquiryQuestion: From which earlier languages did scholars at the House of Wisdom translate science and medical scrolls?
milestones.imageCaption: Scholars reading and debating stacked Arabic manuscripts inside a Baghdad library (painted by Yahya al-Wasiti, AD 1237).
milestones.provenance: Bibliothèque nationale de France / Public Domain (Wikimedia Commons)
milestones.catalyst: Caliph al-Ma’mun expanded Baghdad’s House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma), where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars like Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Greek, Persian, and Indian scrolls into Arabic—while the Banu Musa brothers invented 100 automatic machines!
milestones.turningPoint: Visitors marvelled at the Banu Musa brothers’ trick water jugs, musical fountains, and self-trimming oil lamps!
milestones.impact: Rescued ancient Euclid, Galen, Hippocrates, and Indian maths from being lost—and tested every idea with fresh experiments.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 820): Al-Khwarizmi Writes Algebra & Champions 0–9 Numerals.

ks2.story: Caliph al-Ma’mun expanded Baghdad’s House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma), where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars like Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Greek, Persian, and Indian scrolls into Arabic—while the Banu Musa brothers invented 100 automatic machines!
ks2.significance: Rescued ancient Euclid, Galen, Hippocrates, and Indian maths from being lost—and tested every idea with fresh experiments.
ks2.childrenLife: Visitors marvelled at the Banu Musa brothers’ trick water jugs, musical fountains, and self-trimming oil lamps!
ks2.quote: “Legend says Hunayn ibn Ishaq’s careful medical translations were rewarded with their weight in gold!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: From which earlier languages did scholars at the House of Wisdom translate science and medical scrolls?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Ancient Greek, Syriac, Persian, and Indian Sanskrit—all translated into clear Arabic!

milestones.title: Al-Khwarizmi Writes Algebra & Champions 0–9 Numerals
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which two modern maths/computing words come directly from Al-Khwarizmi’s book title and his own name?
milestones.imageCaption: Medieval Arabic manuscript page from Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi’s foundational book on algebra (al-Jabr).
milestones.catalyst: Working in Baghdad, mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi explained Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9 with place value) and wrote his famous book al-Jabr ("balancing equations") to solve land, trade, and inheritance problems!
milestones.turningPoint: Instead of wrestling with clumsy Roman numerals like CLXVIII, students lined up neat tens, hundreds, and zeros in seconds.
milestones.impact: Gave the modern world "algebra", "zero" (from Arabic sifr), and "algorithm" (from Al-Khwarizmi’s own name)—powering every computer today!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 850–920): Silk Road Caravanserais, Dhows & Silver Dirhams in Viking Britain!.

ks2.story: Working in Baghdad, mathematician Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi explained Hindu-Arabic numerals (0–9 with place value) and wrote his famous book al-Jabr ("balancing equations") to solve land, trade, and inheritance problems!
ks2.significance: Gave the modern world "algebra", "zero" (from Arabic sifr), and "algorithm" (from Al-Khwarizmi’s own name)—powering every computer today!
ks2.childrenLife: Instead of wrestling with clumsy Roman numerals like CLXVIII, students lined up neat tens, hundreds, and zeros in seconds.
ks2.quote: “Every smartphone, search engine, and video game runs step-by-step ‘algorithms’ named after Al-Khwarizmi of Baghdad!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Which two modern maths/computing words come directly from Al-Khwarizmi’s book title and his own name?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: "Algebra" (from al-Jabr) and "Algorithm" (from the Latin spelling of Al-Khwarizmi)!

milestones.title: Silk Road Caravanserais, Dhows & Silver Dirhams in Viking Britain!
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did silver dirham coins minted in Baghdad and Samarkand end up buried in Viking England?
milestones.imageCaption: Pure silver Abbasid dirham coin struck with Kufic Arabic script—found in hoards as far away as Viking Yorkshire.
milestones.catalyst: Camel caravans resting at stone caravanserais and lateen-sailed wooden dhows brought Chinese silk, Indonesian spices, and African gold to Baghdad—while Viking river traders carried tens of thousands of Islamic silver dirhams right to Jorvik (York) and Cuerdale in England!
milestones.turningPoint: In Baghdad’s scented spice suqs, children smelled cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, and sweet refined sugar.
milestones.impact: Merchants also wrote paper payment notes called sakk (origin of our word "cheque") and Anglo-Saxon King Offa even copied an Abbasid gold dinar!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 900): Physician Al-Razi & Baghdad’s Free Bimaristan Hospitals.

ks2.story: Camel caravans resting at stone caravanserais and lateen-sailed wooden dhows brought Chinese silk, Indonesian spices, and African gold to Baghdad—while Viking river traders carried tens of thousands of Islamic silver dirhams right to Jorvik (York) and Cuerdale in England!
ks2.significance: Merchants also wrote paper payment notes called sakk (origin of our word "cheque") and Anglo-Saxon King Offa even copied an Abbasid gold dinar!
ks2.childrenLife: In Baghdad’s scented spice suqs, children smelled cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, and sweet refined sugar.
ks2.quote: “Finding Baghdad silver dirhams buried in Yorkshire mud proves Early Islamic trade stretched right across medieval Eurasia!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How did silver dirham coins minted in Baghdad and Samarkand end up buried in Viking England?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Viking merchants paddled down Russian rivers to trade furs and amber with Muslim traders, bringing silver dirhams back to Scandinavia and England!

milestones.title: Physician Al-Razi & Baghdad’s Free Bimaristan Hospitals
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What clever experiment did doctor Al-Razi use to pick the healthiest location for Baghdad’s hospital?
milestones.imageCaption: Carved monumental stone entrance of a medieval Islamic teaching hospital (bimaristan).
milestones.catalyst: To pick the cleanest air in Baghdad for a new hospital, physician Al-Razi hung fresh meat in different neighbourhoods and chose the spot where it rotted slowest! Baghdad’s bimaristans treated men and women, rich and poor, completely free in separate clean wards.
milestones.turningPoint: Recovering patients rested beside cooling courtyard fountains with fresh fruit, pharmacies, and trainee medical students.
milestones.impact: Al-Razi wrote the first clear medical account distinguishing smallpox from measles, while Al-Zahrawi illustrated over 200 surgical tools and catgut stitches.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 900–950): Geometric Star Tiles, Golden Lustreware, Hammams & Chess.

ks2.story: To pick the cleanest air in Baghdad for a new hospital, physician Al-Razi hung fresh meat in different neighbourhoods and chose the spot where it rotted slowest! Baghdad’s bimaristans treated men and women, rich and poor, completely free in separate clean wards.
ks2.significance: Al-Razi wrote the first clear medical account distinguishing smallpox from measles, while Al-Zahrawi illustrated over 200 surgical tools and catgut stitches.
ks2.childrenLife: Recovering patients rested beside cooling courtyard fountains with fresh fruit, pharmacies, and trainee medical students.
ks2.quote: “Bimaristans never turned away a poor traveller—and even gave recovering patients a small sum of coins when they went home!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What clever experiment did doctor Al-Razi use to pick the healthiest location for Baghdad’s hospital?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: He hung pieces of fresh meat around the city and built the hospital where the meat rotted slowest (showing the cleanest, freshest air)!

milestones.title: Geometric Star Tiles, Golden Lustreware, Hammams & Chess
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Name three foods or everyday items enjoyed in AD 900 Baghdad that were almost unknown in Anglo-Saxon Britain.
milestones.imageCaption: Interlocking glazed ceramic star-and-polygon geometric tilework crafted with ruler and compasses.
milestones.provenance: Museum Islamic Art Collection / Public Domain (Wikimedia Commons)
milestones.catalyst: Using geometry, artisans tiled walls with endless interlocking stars, leafy arabesques, Kufic calligraphy, and metallic lustreware bowls—while families washed with perfumed hard soap at tiled hammams, ate oranges and rice, and played shatranj (chess)!
milestones.turningPoint: In shaded courtyard homes cooled by windcatchers, children moved carved ceramic shatranj chess pieces and listened to Sinbad tales!
milestones.impact: Introduced citrus fruits, aubergines, spinach, sugar, hard soap, lustre glass, and One Thousand and One Nights storytelling.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 950–964): Mariam al-Asturlabi’s Brass Astrolabes & Al-Sufi’s Star Book.

ks2.significance: Introduced citrus fruits, aubergines, spinach, sugar, hard soap, lustre glass, and One Thousand and One Nights storytelling.
ks2.childrenLife: In shaded courtyard homes cooled by windcatchers, children moved carved ceramic shatranj chess pieces and listened to Sinbad tales!
ks2.quote: “Because mosques avoided statues of people or animals, artists turned geometry, plants, and Arabic script into breathtaking art.”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Name three foods or everyday items enjoyed in AD 900 Baghdad that were almost unknown in Anglo-Saxon Britain.
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Sweet oranges/lemons, rice, refined sugar, aubergines, perfumed hard soap, paper books, and shatranj (chess)!

milestones.title: Mariam al-Asturlabi’s Brass Astrolabes & Al-Sufi’s Star Book
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What three practical things could a traveller or astronomer work out using a brass astrolabe?
milestones.imageCaption: Finely engraved medieval Islamic brass planispheric astrolabe used to measure star heights, time, and direction.
milestones.provenance: Museum of the History of Science / CC0 / Public Domain (Wikimedia Commons)
milestones.catalyst: Master instrument-makers such as Mariam al-Asturlabi in Aleppo crafted intricate pocket-sized brass astrolabes—acting like ancient sky-computers to tell time, find prayer direction toward Mecca, and guide ships—while Al-Sufi mapped constellations and the Andromeda Galaxy!
milestones.turningPoint: Apprentices learned to line up the brass sighting rule (alidade) with the North Star or daytime sun.
milestones.impact: Dozens of bright stars on modern astronomy charts—Aldebaran, Betelgeuse, Rigel, Vega, Altair—still carry their Arabic names today!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. AD 1011–1025): Ibn al-Haytham’s Pinhole Camera & Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine.

ks2.story: Master instrument-makers such as Mariam al-Asturlabi in Aleppo crafted intricate pocket-sized brass astrolabes—acting like ancient sky-computers to tell time, find prayer direction toward Mecca, and guide ships—while Al-Sufi mapped constellations and the Andromeda Galaxy!
ks2.significance: Dozens of bright stars on modern astronomy charts—Aldebaran, Betelgeuse, Rigel, Vega, Altair—still carry their Arabic names today!
ks2.childrenLife: Apprentices learned to line up the brass sighting rule (alidade) with the North Star or daytime sun.
ks2.quote: “In AD 964 astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi recorded a ‘little cloud’ in Andromeda—the earliest written record of another galaxy!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What three practical things could a traveller or astronomer work out using a brass astrolabe?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Exact time of day or night, latitude/position for navigation, and the direction (qibla) of Mecca!

milestones.title: Ibn al-Haytham’s Pinhole Camera & Ibn Sina’s Canon of Medicine
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What false ancient belief about eyesight did Ibn al-Haytham disprove with his dark-room pinhole experiments?
milestones.imageCaption: Medieval Arabic scientific manuscript diagram illustrating the anatomy of the human eyes and optic nerves.
milestones.catalyst: Testing light beams through a tiny hole into a dark room (al-bayt al-muzlim -> camera obscura), Ibn al-Haytham proved light travels in straight lines FROM objects INTO our eyes! Meanwhile Ibn Sina completed his five-volume Canon of Medicine.
milestones.turningPoint: Watching upside-down candle flames projected through a pinhole proved ancient Greek myths of "eye-beams" were wrong!
milestones.impact: Ibn al-Haytham pioneered the experimental scientific method and cameras; Ibn Sina’s Canon taught doctors across Islam and Europe for 500 years!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (February AD 1258): Mongol Siege of Baghdad (1258) & Survival of Golden Age Ideas.

ks2.story: Testing light beams through a tiny hole into a dark room (al-bayt al-muzlim -> camera obscura), Ibn al-Haytham proved light travels in straight lines FROM objects INTO our eyes! Meanwhile Ibn Sina completed his five-volume Canon of Medicine.
ks2.significance: Ibn al-Haytham pioneered the experimental scientific method and cameras; Ibn Sina’s Canon taught doctors across Islam and Europe for 500 years!
ks2.childrenLife: Watching upside-down candle flames projected through a pinhole proved ancient Greek myths of "eye-beams" were wrong!
ks2.quote: “The seeker after truth does not put blind faith in old books, but questions and tests every claim by experiment!” — Ibn al-Haytham
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What false ancient belief about eyesight did Ibn al-Haytham disprove with his dark-room pinhole experiments?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: He disproved the belief that invisible rays shot OUT of human eyes—proving instead that light bounces OFF objects INTO our eyes!

milestones.date: End of Abbasid Baghdad & Global Legacy
milestones.title: Mongol Siege of Baghdad (1258) & Survival of Golden Age Ideas
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why didn’t all the scientific discoveries of the Islamic Golden Age disappear when Baghdad fell in AD 1258?
milestones.imageCaption: Fourteenth-century Persian miniature showing Hulagu Khan’s Mongol army besieging walled Baghdad across the Tigris in AD 1258.
milestones.provenance: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin / Public Domain (Wikimedia Commons)
milestones.catalyst: In February AD 1258, Hulagu Khan’s Mongol siege engines breached Baghdad’s walls, destroying canals and the House of Wisdom. Yet Islamic scholarship survived—400,000 books were saved for Maragheh, Cairo thrived, and translations in Spain (Córdoba & Toledo) sparked Europe’s Renaissance!
milestones.turningPoint: Students at new universities in Oxford, Paris, and Bologna studied Latin translations of Al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina, and Ibn al-Haytham!
milestones.impact: Explains why 0–9 numerals, algebra, algorithms, optics, hospitals, and words like chemistry, zero, orange, and sofa live on worldwide.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Completes all 10 turning points in Early Islamic Civilisation & Baghdad (c. AD 750–1258).

ks2.significance: Explains why 0–9 numerals, algebra, algorithms, optics, hospitals, and words like chemistry, zero, orange, and sofa live on worldwide.
ks2.childrenLife: Students at new universities in Oxford, Paris, and Bologna studied Latin translations of Al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina, and Ibn al-Haytham!
ks2.quote: “One siege ended Abbasid Baghdad—yet copied paper books carried its Golden Age science across every ocean!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why didn’t all the scientific discoveries of the Islamic Golden Age disappear when Baghdad fell in AD 1258?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Paper copies had already spread to libraries in Cairo, Maragheh, Damascus, Sicily, and Al-Andalus (Spain), where translators shared them into Latin!
